newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russia still has rocky road to economic growth.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russia still has rocky road to economic growth.

text.p: The road to Russian economic recovery has been paved with bold forecasts and good intentions, but the long-awaited turnaround remains just out of sight after five years of market-oriented economic reforms.

Inflation is at record lows, the International Monetary Fund has resumed lending after two gaps in the second half of the year and the rouble has held firmly within a gently sloping downward corridor against the dollar.

But millions of Russians survive on less than $100 a month -- if they get paid at all -- and tax evasion is rampant. Miners struck this month because they had not received wages and the government stopped spending money because coffers were bare.
Gross domestic product, a broad measure of the size of economic output, is stubbornly below 1995 levels, despite many official predictions that the economy is poised for growth.
REFORMS HARD AND DIFFICULT

"Reforms are not going easily, they are hard and difficult, It is difficult today for everyone in Russia," Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told workers as the first Russian-assembled Western car rolled off the production line in the autonomous region of Tatarstan this month.

"But we are already moving beyond this difficulty to a new order... 1997 will be a different year for us, a breakthrough. A breakthrough in that we will no longer prepare, but will strengthen the economy."
Chernomyrdin, a gas industry manager turned politician, has taken much of the credit for tough monetary policies designed to drive Russian inflation down.
Consumer prices are expected to rise about 22 percent this year, after a rise of 130 percent in the year to December 1995 and rates of around 2,000 percent in the first year of reforms.
But there have been few moves to restructure the inefficient companies inherited from Soviet days and many company managers are nostalgic for handouts they received then.

Investment is low, partly because companies cannot afford to borrow at Russia's still high interest rates and partly because foreign firms are frightened away by frequently changing legislation and fear of political unrest.
COMMUNISTS MAY LOSE TASTE FOR BATTLE

The Communists are the biggest party in the lower house of parliament and President Boris Yeltsin needed all his strength -- and a generous injection of budget funds -- to fight off a Communist challenger in July's presidential election.

Many economists say the high pre-election spending was at the root of the problems with the IMF in the second half of the year. Expensive promises made during the campaign were quietly forgotten as Yeltsin disappeared into a series of government rest homes to prepare for an operation on his heart.

But the Communists appear to have lost their taste for a battle and parliament approved the first two readings of a tight 1997 budget this month, giving Yeltsin a welcome fillip in time for his return to the Kremlin.

The president, who had his third heart attack between the two rounds of the presidential election, had a quintuple bypass operation on November 5 and has spent most of the last six months in hospital or in rest homes.
In his first television address since his operation, Yeltsin said tax collection and non-payments would be among his priorities after he returned.
"Many problems have accumulated which need the president's intervention," he said.

"A state that cannot pay its workers for labour they have performed -- this simply cannot be allowed...I would like to remind managers of enterprises -- if you are unable to pay (taxes) that means you are unfit for the job.
"And if you are unfit, you have to go."
YELTSIN HINTS AT GOVERNMENT CHANGES
Yeltsin also hinted at changes to his government, accusing some officials of easing up while he was away.
"The only criteria here is the quality of life of the people," he said. "We will part with those who are unable to turn towards the people. We need new impulses, we need more courage and energy."

Yeltsin did not say which ministers might go, but the Russian media have blamed Finance Minister Alexander Livshits for the tax and wage fiascos and the Communists have made no secret of their hatred for presidential chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais.

Yeltsin dumped then privatisation chief Chubais unceremoniously in January after the Communists' strong showing in 1995 parliamentary elections, accusing him of destroying the value of peoples' savings and of selling industry for a song.
But he brought the ginger-haired economist back to the Kremlin after the July presidential poll, before which Chubais had played a major role in raising funds.

Opponents say Chubais has acted as regent while Yeltsin was ill. The chief-of-staff, also a member of an emergency commission designed to force companies to pay their tax debts, has kept a relatively low profile.
